summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Banten stands under this national framework. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identity papers, including the national identity card (e-KTP), and Banten is named among the nine provinces whose transgender residents have benefited so far. The stated reasoning was that many of those people were undocumented, particularly where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans traveller, this documents that identity-document issuance for transgender people has operated in this province since mid-2021, which bears on document status and enrolment here.

Provincial criminalisation remains in force in two of Indonesia's provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, which criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Banten is not among them. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and an August 2026 feature reports growing repression against Indonesia's transgender community. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Identity-document access is uneven across Indonesia. The Home Affairs outreach has reached nine provinces: Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. Trans residents outside that list are not documented as covered, so possession of a valid identity card cannot be assumed elsewhere in the country on the strength of Banten's experience.

Document issuance is an administrative measure, not legal recognition of gender. It does not alter the national position that only 'male' and 'female' descriptors exist, and it does not substitute for the surgical and judicial requirements governing legal gender recognition.

The provincial criminalisation layer is concentrated in Aceh and South Sumatra rather than spread across the archipelago, which means a visitor's exposure in Banten derives from national provisions rather than from provincial religious law. The national provisions, including the penal code in force since 2 January 2026 and the 2006 pornography statute, apply everywhere regardless.

Official rhetoric is functioning as an accelerant. Reporting in August 2026 links the rise in attacks on transgender people to public condemnations by officials and to the presidential decree of October 2025 that classifies LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism.

outOfScopeNotes:

Whether the August 2026 reporting on growing repression against transgender people documents specific incidents in Banten is unresolved; the source is cited here for the national pattern only.

Whether the bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour, which was under discussion in 2025, has been enacted is not sourced in this inventory.

Whether the extra-marital sex provision of the 2022 penal code has been used in prosecutions in Banten is not sourced. The inventory characterises prosecutions nationally as selective rather than systematic without provincial breakdown.

Enforcement of the 2006 pornography statute against foreign visitors in Banten, and any local police practice regarding venues or gatherings in this province, are not sourced here.
